'''Fabrizio Carbone''' (born {{Birth date|1976|4|20|df=y}} in [[Novi Ligure]], Italy) is an Italian and Swiss [[physicist]] and currently an associate professor at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne]] (EPFL).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Fabrizio Carbone|url=https://people.epfl.ch/fabrizio.carbone|access-date=2021-02-02|website=people.epfl.ch}}</ref> His research focuses on the study of matter in out of equilibrium conditions using ultrafast spectroscopy, diffraction and imaging techniques.<ref name=":0" /> In 2015, he attracted international attention by publishing a photography of light displaying both its quantum and classical nature.<ref>{{Cite web|title=In Physics First, Light is Captured as Both Particle and Wave|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/science/science-news/physics-first-light-captured-both-particle-wave-n315936|access-date=2021-02-02|website=NBC News|date=2 March 2015 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Dickerson|first=Kelly|title=Scientists take the first ever photograph of light as both a wave and a particle|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/image-of-light-as-a-wave-and-a-particle-2015-3|access-date=2021-02-02|website=Business Insider}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Starr|first=Michelle|title=Scientists capture the first image of light behaving as both a particle and a wave|url=https://www.cnet.com/news/this-is-the-first-photograph-showing-light-as-both-a-particle-and-a-wave/|access-date=2021-02-02|website=CNET|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=No, You Cannot Catch An Individual Photon Acting Simultaneously As A Pure Particle And Wave {{!}} Inside Science|url=http://www.insidescience.org/blog/2015/03/13/no-you-cannot-catch-individual-photon-acting-simultaneously-pure-particle-and-wave|access-date=2021-02-03|website=www.insidescience.org}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Fabrizio Carbone received his master's degree in quantum electronics from the [[University of Pavia]] in 2001, defending a thesis titled 'Characterization of all optical wavelengths converters for telecommunications applications'. He was an industrial researcher at Pirelli Labs between 2000 and 2002, after which he returned to academia and obtained his PhD in condensed matter physics from the [[University of Geneva]] in 2007 defending a thesis titled 'Spectroscopic signatures of electronic correlations in superconductors and magnets' under the supervision of Dirk van der Marel.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Carbone|first=Fabrizio|date=|title=Spectroscopic signatures of electronic correlations in superconductors and magnets|url=http://dqmp.unige.ch/vandermarel/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/thesis_carbone.pdf|access-date=2 February 2021|website=}}</ref> Carbone carried out his postdoctoral appointment at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in the group of Chemistry Nobel Prize laureate [[Ahmed Zewail]]. In 2010, he established the Laboratory for Ultrafast Microscopy and [[Electron scattering|Electron Scattering]] (LUMES) at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]], where he was named tenure track assistant professor in 2011 and promoted to associate professor in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-04-03|title=Eight professors appointed at EPFL |website=École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne |url=https://actu.epfl.ch/news/eight-professors-appointed-at-epfl/|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Fabrizio Carbone promoted Associate Professor of Physics :: NCCR MUST|url=http://www.nccr-must.ch/nccr_must/news_4.html?4329|access-date=2021-02-02|website=www.nccr-must.ch}}</ref>

== Research ==

=== Early career ===
During his PhD in Dirk van der Marel's laboratory at the [[University of Geneva]], Carbone analyzed the interplay between the electronic structure and the magnetism of [[manganese monosilicide]] by means of X-rays and [[neutron spectroscopy]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carbone|first1=F.|last2=Zangrando|first2=M.|last3=Brinkman|first3=A.|last4=Nicolaou|first4=A.|last5=Bondino|first5=F.|last6=Magnano|first6=E.|last7=Nugroho|first7=A. A.|last8=Parmigiani|first8=F.|last9=Jarlborg|first9=Th.|last10=van der Marel|first10=D.|date=2006-02-21|title=Electronic structure of MnSi: The role of electron-electron interactions|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.73.085114|journal=Physical Review B|volume=73|issue=8|article-number=085114|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.73.085114|bibcode=2006PhRvB..73h5114C}}</ref> He also studied the kinetic and potential energy changes associated to the superconducting [[phase transition]] in [[Cuprate|cuprates]] by measuring the material's color changes across the [[Critical point (thermodynamics)|critical temperature]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carbone|first1=F.|last2=Kuzmenko|first2=A. B.|last3=Molegraaf|first3=H. J. A.|last4=van Heumen|first4=E.|last5=Giannini|first5=E.|last6=van der Marel|first6=D.|date=2006-07-06|title=In-plane optical spectral weight transfer in optimally doped Bi<sub>2</sub>⁢Sr<sub>2⁢</sub>Ca<sub>2</sub>⁢Cu<sub>3</sub>⁢O<sub>10</sub>|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.74.024502|journal=Physical Review B|volume=74|issue=2|article-number=024502|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.74.024502|s2cid=55221224|arxiv=cond-mat/0603737}}</ref>

As a [[postdoctoral researcher]] in [[Ahmed Zewail]]'s laboratory at the [[California Institute of Technology]], he developed new methods based on the use of ultrafast electrons and laser pulses for the investigation of materials in out of equilibrium conditions. His most notable result was the demonstration of a new method to perform femtosecond-resolved [[electron spectroscopy]] in a [[Transmission electron microscopy|Transmission Electron microscope]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carbone|first1=Fabrizio|last2=Kwon|first2=Oh-Hoon|last3=Zewail|first3=Ahmed H.|date=2009-07-10|title=Dynamics of Chemical Bonding Mapped by Energy-Resolved 4D Electron Microscopy|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1175005|journal=Science|language=en|volume=325|issue=5937|pages=181–184|doi=10.1126/science.1175005|issn=0036-8075|pmid=19589997|bibcode=2009Sci...325..181C|s2cid=206520587|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This technique opened a new field of research in the following years leading to several breakthroughs in the observation of materials, molecules and nanostructures under laser irradiation conditions.

=== Current activities ===
Carbone currently heads the Laboratory for Ultrafast Microscopy and Electron Scattering (LUMES) at [[École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne|EPFL]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=LUMES|url=https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lumes/|access-date=2021-02-02|website=www.epfl.ch|language=en-GB}}</ref> The LUMES is active in various research fields:<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Research|url=https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lumes/research/|access-date=2021-02-02|website=www.epfl.ch|language=en-GB}}</ref>
* Physics of phase transitions in strongly correlated solids: in this area, the group of Prof. Carbone reported the first real-time observation of the coherent oscillations of a superconducting condensate triggered by the superconducting to normal-state phase transition-induced laser pulses.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mansart|first1=Barbara|last2=Lorenzana|first2=José|last3=Mann|first3=Andreas|last4=Odeh|first4=Ahmad|last5=Scarongella|first5=Mariateresa|last6=Chergui|first6=Majed|last7=Carbone|first7=Fabrizio|date=2013-03-19|title=Coupling of a high-energy excitation to superconducting quasiparticles in a cuprate from coherent charge fluctuation spectroscopy|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=110|issue=12|pages=4539–4544|doi=10.1073/pnas.1218742110|bibcode=2013PNAS..110.4539M|s2cid=118367698|issn=0027-8424|pmc=3606993|doi-access=free }}</ref>
* Imaging and controlling nano-confined electromagnetic fields: various new methods were developed to obtain real-space/real-time movies of light confined in nanostructures. These results are of particular importance both for fundamental aspects and applications in optoelectronic devices.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Piazza|first1=L.|last2=Lummen|first2=T. T. == Recognition ==
Carbone was awarded the 2016 University Latsis Prize.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Marti-Rochat|first=Patricia|date=2016-03-10|title=University Latsis Award EPFL 2016 – Fabrizio Carbone |website=École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne |url=https://actu.epfl.ch/news/university-latsis-award-epfl-2016-fabrizio-carbone/|language=en}}</ref> He received a Starting Grant (2010) and a Consolidator Grant (2017) from the [[European Research Council]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=ERC FUNDED PROJECTS|url=https://erc.europa.eu/projects-figures/erc-funded-projects/results|access-date=2021-02-02|website=ERC: European Research Council|language=en|archive-date=2021-01-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210113223931/https://erc.europa.eu/projects-figures/erc-funded-projects/results}}</ref> He was named a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 2022 "for pioneering work using ultrafast electron scattering instrumentation to discover and control new states of matter at the nanometer and sub-femtosecond scales".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2022|title=Fellows nominated in 2022|work=APS Fellows archive|publisher=American Physical Society|access-date=2022-10-19}}</ref>
